Primary evidence with patient variants includes Tummala et al. (PMID 24507776; three index cases with BMF and neurological dysfunction, homozygous truncating mutations), Zhang et al. (PMID 27185855; homozygous nonsense ERCC6L2 mutation with mild BMF and microcephaly), Shabanova et al. (PMID 29633571; additional case plus five previously reported), Tummala et al. (PMID 29987015; eight cases from five families), and Bluteau/Douglas cohorts (PMIDs 29146883, 36952636) with dozens of affected individuals and a founder mutation. Functional work supports a mechanism (transcription-coupled repair/R-loop resolution, impaired erythropoiesis), reinforcing causality. This is replicated, human, single-gene-level evidence, so Established is strongly favored; a small residual probability reflects that some series describe purely hematologic phenotypes without developmental delay.

Multiple independent human studies report causal AICDA variants in patients with hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 in their own results: the original identification of AID mutations in HIGM2 patients (PMID 11007475), a homozygous founder variant p.Met139Thr in Finnish families (PMID 27142677), a novel homozygous splice-site variant c.428-1G>T in two siblings (PMID 35246784), a novel homozygous missense variant in Brazilian sisters (PMID 23803409), several novel/recurrent AICDA mutations in 11 Tunisian patients (PMID 26545377), and heterozygous C-terminal variants causing autosomal dominant HIGM2 (PMIDs 15893695, 38363477). Additional case reports (PMIDs 36931691, 27789066, 19575287) further replicate the finding across unrelated probands with functional evidence of impaired class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation. Mouse and biochemical studies (PMIDs 18716662, 22715099, 33098766) provide supporting mechanism but are not needed for the human causal claim. The evidence is unambiguous and extensively replicated, so Established is overwhelmingly favored.

phenotype: X-linked central congenital hypothyroidism with late-onset testicular enlargement
justification: Multiple independent human studies report loss-of-function point variants in IGSF1 in unrelated probands and families with X-linked central congenital hypothyroidism with macroorchidism/delayed testosterone rise: three novel mutations in four Japanese boys (PMID 23966245), a novel insertion mutation causing a premature stop (PMID 23363888), a novel mutation segregating in a large Irish kindred (PMID 30086211), a novel variant in a French family (PMID 35350016), a novel nonsense variant in Japanese siblings (PMID 38299175), two novel mutations in three patients (PMID 38295770), and a novel nonsense variant p.Q1187* (PMID 35466665). These are sequence-level variants in the gene itself, not multigene deletions, and are replicated across independent cohorts and countries; large phenotyping series (PMID 24108313) and national surveys (PMID 38462462) confirm IGSF1 as the most common genetic cause of isolated central CH. Functional work (PMID 28262687, 31650157) provides mechanistic support via pituitary TRHR/FSHB regulation. The evidence is therefore clearly Established.

Multiple independent human reports present their own primary genetic findings of germline SDHB mutations in patients with the GIST–paraganglioma dyad: PMID 36387130 (case with bladder paraganglioma plus SDH-deficient GIST and germline SDHB mutation), PMID 20890271 (germline SDHB p.Ser92Thr identified in a Carney-Stratakis patient with SDHB-negative GIST), and PMID 20119652 (pathogenic SDHB mutation in a patient with two components of the Carney triad/Carney-Stratakis spectrum). Additional supporting primary data come from germline SDHB mutations detected in wild-type GIST cohorts (PMIDs 21173220, 22948025, 31883676, 22160509), consistent with incomplete-penetrance CSS phenotypes. Reviews (19522824, 34012423, 28739378) restate the SDHB/SDHC/SDHD basis of CSS as established background. Since at least two independent probands with point mutations (not multigene deletions) are reported in their own results, the Established category is well supported; a small residual weight is left for Existing given that several key reports are single cases.

Several primary human genetic studies report causative TAZ/TAFAZZIN (G4.5) variants in independent Barth syndrome probands and families: PMID 9382096 identified mutations in nine of eleven familial cases of BTHS/X-linked cardiomyopathy; PMID 10484795 found G4.5 mutations in five unrelated families with suspected Barth syndrome; PMID 12032589 reported a novel missense R94S mutation in a Japanese boy with the full BTHS phenotype; and PMID 9382097 and PMID 11238270 describe additional novel mutations in allelic left ventricular noncompaction/BTHS patients. These are point mutations in a single gene, not multigene copy number changes, and they replicate across independent cohorts and populations. Functional and biochemical work (cardiolipin/monolysocardiolipin abnormalities, tafazzin transacylase activity) corroborates the mechanism, and reviews consistently describe TAFAZZIN as the sole known cause of BTHS. The evidence therefore clearly meets the Established threshold.

Multiple independent human studies report distinct pathogenic AP3B1 variants in unrelated HPS2 probands: PMID 11809908 identified two nonsense mutations (C1578T, G2028T) with complete loss of β3A protein; PMID 31820501 reported novel compound heterozygous mutations (p.M63K, p.L849X) in a Japanese patient; PMID 28585318 described five unreported cases with four novel mutations including a splice-altering variant; PMID 23215637 found a novel frameshift deletion (c.3222_3223delTG); and PMID 16551969 reported a novel homozygous AP3B1 mutation. Additional independent cohorts (PMID 36162005, Oman) and structural mechanisms (PMID 23557002 inversion) further replicate the causal link, and functional work shows AP-3 complex loss explains albinism, neutropenia, platelet dense granule and cytotoxic lymphocyte defects (PMIDs 14566336, 17931556). The mouse pearl model (PMID 9931340) supports the mechanism but is not needed given abundant human point-mutation evidence. Evidence is replicated across independent families and ethnicities, satisfying the criteria for Established.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary evidence of biallelic IL11RA variants causing craniosynostosis with dental anomalies: Nieminen et al. (PMID 21741611) identified homozygous missense/nonsense/duplication variants segregating in five unrelated consanguineous families with craniosynostosis, delayed tooth eruption and supernumerary teeth, with functional loss-of-function demonstration; Keupp et al. (PMID 24498618) found segregating splice, missense and nonsense mutations in six additional families with Crouzon-like craniosynostosis plus functional STAT3 assays; Brischoux-Boucher et al. (PMID 29926465) described 10 further patients with six missense variants; Kespohl et al. (PMID 37596289) reported a novel homozygous p.W307R in two siblings with functional validation; additional independent probands are reported in PMIDs 30811827, 35331937 and 40353334. Supporting mouse Il11ra-null and IL6ST models corroborate the mechanism but are not needed for the human causal claim. This constitutes replicated, gene-specific (non-CNV) human evidence, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic KIT point mutations segregating with piebaldism in unrelated probands and families: Spritz et al. (PMID 1370874) identified a missense Phe584Leu and two frameshifts in three patients; Giebel & Spritz (PMID 1376329) found Glu583Lys in an affected kindred; Syrris et al. (PMID 12204004) reported six novel KIT mutations in three families and three isolated cases; Spritz et al. (PMID 7529964) found KIT mutations in ~75% of 28 typical piebaldism patients; and further reports include splice-site and de novo missense variants (PMIDs 24000325, 32220041, 33194047, 38887855). These are human genetic studies with variants detected in patients, not merely background citations or copy-number events, and the murine W/dominant-spotting phenotype supports the mechanism. Evidence is strong, replicated, and mutation-type/phenotype correlations are documented, so the relationship is Established.

Aldahmesh et al. (PMID 23830514) identified homozygous truncating LRPAP1 variants in consanguineous families with Mendelian high myopia via exome/autozygome analysis, with supporting functional data (LRP1 deficiency, TGF-β upregulation). Independent human cohorts and clinical series replicate and extend this: clinical characterization of LRPAP1-related pediatric high myopia (PMID 26271838), childhood-onset rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in patients with recessive LRPAP1 mutations (PMID 31607522), additional probands from early-onset high myopia exome screening (PMID 25525168), and further homozygous-variant cases (PMIDs 39444998, 40725504). Zebrafish and stem-cell knockout studies (PMIDs 36261846, 34469777) provide mechanistic support but are not needed for the human genetic evidence. Several listed papers (Alzheimer's cholesterol shuttle, cathepsin D ERT, lanoteplase disposition) are incidental co-mentions of LRPAP1 unrelated to myopia.

Multiple independent primary reports identify biallelic SLC24A5 variants in unrelated human probands with non-syndromic OCA6: the original exome-sequencing discovery paper (23364476, c.591G>A and c.1361insT), two novel frameshift variants in two unrelated Chinese patients (31486119), a Japanese compound heterozygous patient with c.590+1dupG/p.G200R (34870899), and three large consanguineous Pakistani families with segregating missense/frameshift alleles (32274888). Additional independent reports include a homozygous SLC24A5 insertion in an Indian patient (23010199), a homozygous mutation in French Guiana patients (26491832), and the first Italian OCA6 case (26686029). Functional work (in vitro transport assays, zebrafish and knock-in mouse models) corroborates the loss-of-function mechanism, and large cohort screens list SLC24A5 as an established OCA gene. This constitutes replicated human evidence in independent families for a causal gene–disease relationship.

The seminal report by Lindhurst et al. (PMID 21793738) identified a mosaic activating AKT1 c.49G>A (p.Glu17Lys) variant in affected tissues of multiple independent patients with Proteus syndrome, with unaffected tissues lacking the variant. Independent replication comes from PMID 23436452 (high-level mosaicism of AKT1 c.49G>A detected in epidermal nevus scrapings of multiple patients), PMID 24387135 (a separate proband with somatic activating AKT1 mutation), PMID 35799996 (postmortem molecular confirmation in brain tissue of a new case), and PMID 41368924 (7/7 sequenced paratesticular tumors from a cohort carrying AKT1 c.49G>A). All evidence is human, involves a specific single-nucleotide somatic variant (not a multigene copy number change), and is further supported by targeted AKT-inhibitor therapy trials (PMIDs 32014856, 40713644). This constitutes strong, replicated causal evidence.

phenotype: intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities
justification: Multiple independent human cohorts report de novo point/truncating variants in FBXO11 in probands with intellectual disability, dysmorphic facies, and behavioral abnormalities: Gregor et al. (PMID 30057029, 20 individuals), Jansen et al. (PMID 30679813, 24 individuals), Fritzen et al. (PMID 29796876, 2 unrelated individuals), and Gregor et al. follow-up with functional evidence of loss of function (PMID 34505148, 23 additional individuals). Further replication comes from Chinese families (PMID 38740982), a familial inherited case with a novel frameshift variant (PMID 32902151), and additional case reports (PMIDs 38679370, 35940561, 41230589). Functional studies show mislocalization/reduced protein levels supporting haploinsufficiency, consistent with the genetic data. Otitis media association papers concern a distinct phenotype and the suicidal behavior/ASD GWAS papers are incidental, but they do not detract from the abundant IDDFBA evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic loss-of-function variants in PPP1R13L in patients with severe early-onset dilated/arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with ectodermal features. PMID 28069640 first identified a homozygous premature stop codon in five infants from four Arab Christian families, with functional validation in patient fibroblasts and mouse models. PMID 32666529 independently identified biallelic PPP1R13L variants in seven children from five unrelated families via GeneMatcher, explicitly establishing a robust gene–disease association. Further independent probands/families are reported in PMIDs 37698259, 35924320, 39579152, 35933355, and 41919412, demonstrating replication with phenotypic expansion. The wa3 mouse model (PMID 15661756) provides concordant animal evidence, while the lung cancer/AML papers concern unrelated phenotypes.

Several human studies report DCLRE1C (ARTEMIS) variants in patients presenting with Omenn syndrome or Omenn-like radiosensitive SCID: the Saudi cohort explicitly analyzed T-B-NK+ SCID and Omenn syndrome cases with mutations in RAG1, RAG2 or DCLRE1C (PMID 19912631); the TREC/KREC study included molecularly confirmed SCID/Omenn syndrome patients with DCLRE1C mutations (PMID 32691468); and a case report describes compound heterozygous DCLRE1C mutations with an Omenn-syndrome-like clinical picture (PMID 34406419). Additional cohorts (Kuwait DNA-recombination defects with Omenn syndrome cases including DCLRE1C deficiency, PMID 29051008; Turkish SCID/Omenn panel, PMID 32445296) and a structural study of an RS-SCID Omenn variant (PMID 34387696) reinforce the link, though several sources restate the association as background (PMIDs 19953608, 26476407) rather than providing primary Omenn genotype–phenotype data. Because the strongest evidence often groups Omenn patients with other SCID genes without unambiguous per-patient genotype assignment, some probability remains on "Existing" rather than fully replicated "Established". Non-human/in vitro work only supports mechanism, so little weight goes to "Hypothesized".

Multiple independent human studies report de novo or segregating pathogenic single-nucleotide/indel variants in CHD2 in patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE94). Primary evidence includes targeted resequencing identifying de novo CHD2 mutations as a new cause of epileptic encephalopathy (PMID 23708187), a de novo frameshift in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (PMID 24614520), 17 patients with 16 mostly de novo variants (PMID 31677157), three novel loss-of-function variants with molecular splicing analysis in Chinese patients (PMID 35627293), 18 new patients plus review of 84 (PMID 34713950), and a three-generation family with a segregating nonsense variant (PMID 38125503). Additional multicenter cohorts and case series (PMIDs 40934838, 39035822, 35386198) replicate the association across independent probands, and functional/methylation-episignature work supports the mechanism. This constitutes strong, replicated human evidence of causation.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic CRB2 variants in patients with the ventriculomegaly/cystic (Finnish-type nephrosis-like) kidney disease phenotype. Slavotinek et al. (25557780) described five fetuses and a child from three families with cerebral ventriculomegaly, echogenic/microcystic kidneys and raised MSAFP, with compound heterozygous/homozygous CRB2 variants identified by exome sequencing. Jaron et al. (26925547) and Ebarasi/Slavotinek follow-ups (27004616) added new probands, and 32051522 reported a Chinese family with two affected fetuses and novel compound heterozygous variants used for preimplantation testing. Further replication comes from 36071576 (six new patients plus review of 28) and 36803301 (three cases from two families with hydrocephalus and renal cysts, with neuropathological characterization). These are independent probands with single-gene point/indel variants, satisfying criteria for an Established gene–disease relationship.

phenotype: congenital microcephaly - severe encephalopathy - progressive cerebral atrophy syndrome
justification: The original discovery paper (PMID 24139043) identified recessive ASNS mutations in four independent families with congenital microcephaly, progressive cerebral atrophy and intractable seizures, supported by functional data and a hypomorphic mouse model. Multiple independent human reports since then have replicated the finding with novel biallelic variants in unrelated probands and families: an Emirati family (PMID 25227173), two Indian consanguineous families (PMID 30978478), a homozygous mutation in sisters with expanded phenotype (PMID 27469131), siblings with Arg49Gln plus fibroblast functional studies (PMID 29279279), Turkish siblings (PMID 31123592), Japanese patients (PMID 27743885), an Egyptian family (PMID 33271615), and additional novel variants (PMIDs 30057589, 37900678). Genotype–phenotype correlation, segregation in consanguineous families, and enzymatic/cellular functional validation all support causation. This is a well-established autosomal recessive gene–disease relationship (OMIM #615574).

Two independent primary human cohorts demonstrate causality with patient-level variants: Narumi et al. (PMID 27182967) identified de novo SAMD9 mutations in 11 patients with adrenal hypoplasia and defined MIRAGE syndrome, with functional confirmation of gain-of-function growth restriction; Buonocore et al. (PMID 28346228) independently found de novo heterozygous SAMD9 mutations in 8 additional children with the same multisystem phenotype. Further independent probands and families with specific point variants are reported (PMID 29175836, 30403727, 31572304, 38213203, 37195360, 39348076, 31620126), including inheritance modified by revertant mosaicism. Consensus/classification reviews (PMIDs 36445482, 38649131) recognize SAMD9 gain-of-function as the cause of MIRAGE syndrome. Evidence is human, replicated, and single-gene resolution, so "Established" is clearly warranted.

Multiple independent human reports identify non-mosaic hypomorphic EBP variants in males with MEND syndrome: PMID 39754633 reports a novel pathogenic EBP variant in a family with two affected patients, PMID 24459067 identifies a novel hemizygous p.W47R EBP variant segregating in four affected males over three generations with characteristic sterol abnormalities, and PMID 31397093 reports a family with MEND syndrome carrying a hypomorphic EBP mutation with modifier analysis. PMID 22229330 further delineates MEND as a distinct male EBP-disorder phenotype versus Conradi-Hünermann-Happle syndrome. Supporting biochemical/functional evidence (accumulation of 8-dehydrocholesterol and cholest-8(9)-enol, sterol isomerase deficiency) corroborates causality in humans. Several other listed papers concern CDPX2/EBP in females or are homonymous "EBP" (elastin binding protein, exosome binding peptide) and were dismissed.

The original discovery study (PMID 22265015) identified de novo heterozygous truncating SRCAP mutations clustered in the final exon in 13 unrelated individuals with Floating-Harbor syndrome, and this was independently replicated by PMID 22965468 (de novo exon 34 truncating variants in 6/9 FHS patients), PMID 25433523 (expanded exon 33/34 mutation spectrum with follow-up), and PMID 31200758 (novel genotypes in Chinese FHS probands). Additional single-patient reports with molecularly confirmed de novo variants (PMIDs 24375913, 32615693, 38230957, 29383823) further corroborate the genotype–phenotype correlation in humans. Work delineating variant-position-specific DNA methylation signatures (PMID 33909990) shows a clear relationship between location within SRCAP, epigenotype, and FHS versus non-FHS phenotypes, reinforcing causality. All evidence is human, de novo, and replicated across independent cohorts and ethnicities, so the relationship is Established.

Multiple independent human studies report biallelic loss-of-function CCDC88A variants in patients with PEHO-like syndrome: the original consanguineous multiplex family with c.2313delT (PMID 26917597), a Saudi family with a homozygous nonsense variant p.Trp431* (PMID 30392057), an Egyptian family with a novel frameshift p.Thr599ValfsTer4 (PMID 37798908), and an additional novel patient with PEHO-like phenotype and CCDC88A pathogenic variants (PMID 39334473). A further report describes compound heterozygous missense and intragenic deletion variants with functional validation in patient fibroblasts and CRISPR knockouts (PMID 40401444), and a mouse model recapitulates the DEE phenotype (PMIDs 26917597, 39675783), supporting causality. Several other listed papers concern CCDC88A/GIV in cancer, immunity, or signaling and are not relevant to this phenotype. Evidence is replicated across independent probands/families in humans, satisfying criteria for Established.

Multiple independent human studies report causal PIK3R1 variants in SHORT syndrome probands. Dyment/Thauvin-type discovery work includes PMID 23810379 (heterozygous c.1945C>T p.Arg649Trp in two unrelated families with functional validation) and PMID 24886349 (exome sequencing identifying a novel PIK3R1 mutation causing SHORT syndrome). Replication comes from PMID 27766312 (five patients with C-terminal PIK3R1 mutations), and numerous independent probands with distinct variants (PMIDs 33742773, 34026551, 34249805, 35080105, 36515361, 40420664, 40420722). These are single-nucleotide/small variants in humans, not multigene CNVs, and functional data support the mechanism, so the association is firmly established.

The single available article (PMID: 38641995) reports biallelic loss-of-function variants in ZFTRAF1 in humans causing a neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and hypotonia, which is direct human genetic evidence of causality. However, only one publication is provided, so the requirement of at least two independent articles reporting probands/families for "Established" is not met. The evidence is credible and likely multi-family within that single report, but replication across independent publications is lacking, making "Existing" the most appropriate category. Hypothesized and Novel are nearly excluded because direct patient variant data exist rather than merely biological plausibility or incidental co-mention.

Two independent human reports present their own primary patient data with de novo heterozygous ATP2B1 variants: PMID 41223852 ("De novo variants in ATP2B1 lead to neurodevelopmental delay") and PMID 41853798, which identifies a novel de novo c.2140A>C (p.Thr714Pro) in a Chinese proband with infantile spasms and global developmental delay and shows mislocalization and calcium dyshomeostasis in cells. The disorder is an OMIM-recognized entity (MRD66, #619910) with ~12 previously reported de novo pathogenic variants, indicating replication across independent probands. Additional supporting human genetic evidence comes from a biallelic loss-of-function case expanding the phenotype (PMID 37926713) and ATP2B1 variants in epilepsy phenotypes (PMID 40834682), with mechanistic support from PMCA1 calcium-handling biology. Hypertension/GWAS, ARDS, COVID-19 and splicing/PMCA review papers are unrelated to the neurodevelopmental phenotype and do not detract from the causal evidence.

The only primary human genetic evidence is Morimoto et al. (PMID 31004071), which reported a nonsense CFAP43 mutation in a single Japanese family with normal-pressure hydrocephalus, supported by a knockout mouse model showing ventriculomegaly and ciliary abnormalities. The commentary (PMID 33555136) and the systematic review (PMID 40266017) restate this finding as known background and list CFAP43 among NPH risk genes, but they are citations rather than independent replication in new probands or families. Since I cannot cite two independent primary human studies with CFAP43 variants in NPH patients, "Established" cannot be supported. The remaining papers concern CFAP43 in MMAF/sperm flagellar biology or unrelated retinal organoid work and only support the general ciliary mechanism, which underpins a modest "Hypothesized" allocation. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit: one credible human study plus strong ciliary-mechanism support.

PMID 34605855 reports ten affected individuals from seven unrelated families across six countries with biallelic deleterious SLC38A3 (SNAT3) variants and a consistent developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotype, supported by metabolomic evidence of disrupted glutamine/glutamate/histidine metabolism. PMID 36539921 independently reports a novel biallelic nonsense variant in an Indian family with epileptic encephalopathy, providing replication in an independent proband/family. Functional and animal work (PMID 41437789 endothelial Slc38a3 knockout recapitulating postnatal progressive microcephaly and motor dysfunction; PMID 26490457 Snat3 loss-of-function mice with brain glutamine/GABA disturbances) provides a strong mechanistic basis consistent with the human phenotype. Together these constitute strong, replicated human genetic evidence plus supporting model data, meeting the Established criteria.

phenotype: epidermolysis bullosa simplex 6, generalized, with scarring and hair loss
justification: Two independent original discovery papers report causal variants in patients: Lin et al. (PMID 27798626) identified dominant start-codon KLHL24 variants in five EBS patients with functional confirmation of KRT14 degradation, and He et al. (PMID 27889062) found monoallelic c.1A>G/c.2T>C variants in 14 affected individuals from multiple families with a distinct skin-fragility phenotype. Numerous subsequent independent probands and families confirm the association, including de novo variants in Chinese twins (PMID 34804116), Italian cases (PMID 30226531), Russian families (PMID 39135715), and a translation re-initiation variant causing EBS with dilated cardiomyopathy (PMID 35975634). The phenotype described—generalized skin fragility, congenital erosions, burn-like/atrophic scarring, and alopecia (PMID 35066002, 29574966)—matches EBS 6 generalized with scarring and hair loss. Mechanistic human keratinocyte and knock-in mouse studies further corroborate causality, so the evidence is strong and replicated.

Two independent primary studies report ATP1A1 missense variants segregating in multiple human CMT2 families with functional support: PMID 29499166 identified seven missense changes segregating in pedigrees from seven countries, with axolemmal localization and electrophysiological loss-of-function; PMID 31373411 independently found two novel missense variants (p.S207F, p.G877S) in two Chinese intermediate CMT families with degradation/loss-of-function evidence. Additional human cases add replication, including an ATP1A1 p.Pro600Arg patient with progressive motor and sensory neuropathy (PMID 37558483) and further patients with peripheral motor-predominant neuropathy (PMID 35110381). Reviews summarizing ATP1A1-related disease including CMT (PMIDs 34232746, 30842972, 37659504) corroborate but count only as background. The many primary aldosteronism papers are a different phenotype and do not affect this assessment.

Two independent human genetic reports identify causal RBM28 variants in ANE syndrome patients: PMID 18439547 used homozygosity mapping to find a homozygous loss-of-function p.(Leu351Pro) RBM28 mutation in the original family, and PMID 33941690 reported a second, unrelated family/proband with biallelic splice-site variants (c.541+1_541+2delinsA; c.946G>T) with functional validation. PMID 20231366 further characterizes the endocrine phenotype in mutation-carrying patients, supporting clinical replication. Supporting mechanistic work in yeast and human cells (PMIDs 27077951, 25939713, 9312154) explains the ribosomopathy pathophysiology but is not itself the basis for the causal call. Together this constitutes replicated, single-gene-resolution human evidence, meeting the bar for Established, with residual probability given to Existing in case the second family's variants were considered less definitive.

Cousin syndrome is explicitly synonymous with pelviscapular dysplasia (OMIM 260660), and multiple independent human studies report biallelic TBX15 point mutations in affected probands. PMID 19068278 identified two unrelated individuals homozygous for truncating TBX15 mutations with functional evidence of protein destabilization; PMID 24039145 reported an independent patient homozygous for a novel nonsense variant (p.Arg281*); PMID 40693652 described a sixth patient with a novel biallelic missense variant; and PMID 42324217 added three novel individuals from two unrelated families with homozygous TBX15 variants. Additional supportive human phenotyping (PMID 40972941) and the concordant droopy ear mouse model (PMID 14737183) reinforce causality. These are single-gene sequence variants, not multigene deletions, in independent families, satisfying replication criteria for an Established relationship.

Two independent human studies report their own primary genetic findings of heterozygous KRT71 missense variants segregating with autosomal dominant woolly hair/hypotrichosis: Fujimoto et al. in a Japanese family (c.422T>G, p.Phe141Cys, helix initiation motif; PMID 22592156) and a Chinese family with a novel helix termination motif variant (c.1295A>G, p.Tyr432Cys; PMID 41100400), which corresponds to hypotrichosis 13 (HYPT13). A further human case reports a heterozygous intronic KRT71 variant causing loose anagen hair with woolly hair (PMID 40282419), adding an independent proband. Functional support comes from disruption of keratin intermediate filament assembly in cultured cells, a CRISPR Krt71-knockout mouse with woolly hair and hair loss (PMID 37443815), and multiple mammalian models (dog, cat, cattle, mouse) where KRT71 variants cause curly coat, hypotrichosis and IRS dysplasia (PMIDs 34356054, 20953787, 19713490). A commentary explicitly frames KRT71 as an established determinant of human hair texture and woolly hair/hypotrichosis (PMID 22971920). Evidence therefore supports an Established causal relationship, with a small residual probability that reviewers consider human replication limited.

All retrieved articles link PHKG2 exclusively to glycogen storage disease type IX (hepatic phosphorylase kinase deficiency), an autosomal recessive metabolic liver disorder, with additional work on PHKG2 in ferroptosis-related iron regulation. None of the papers mention primary ciliary dyskinesia, ciliary structure/motility, situs abnormalities, bronchiectasis, or any ciliopathy phenotype. PHKG2 is a catalytic gamma subunit of phosphorylase kinase involved in glycogenolysis, providing no plausible mechanistic link to axonemal/ciliary dysfunction. Therefore the evidence supports no relationship between PHKG2 and primary ciliary dyskinesia 33 (co-mentions here are incidental to the query, not to any shared biology).

Multiple independent human reports describe CALM2 variants in patients with a CPVT phenotype: a case report of CPVT with an uncommon CALM2 mutation (PMID 39104518), long-term follow-up of a proband carrying a novel CALM2 c.188C>A p.T63K variant with exercise-induced bidirectional VT (PMID 41550621), two Chinese children with CALM2-related LQTS/CPVT overlap (PMID 42558477), and CALM2 p.N98S carriers with CPVT-like stress-triggered arrest (PMIDs 27100291, 41665141); the International Calmodulinopathy Registry further documents CALM-mediated CPVT across CALM1-3 (PMID 31170290). These are independent probands with single-nucleotide variants, supporting an Established relationship. However, the formal ClinGen-style gene validity reappraisal for CPVT (PMID 34557911) tempers certainty, as CALM2 evidence for CPVT specifically (versus LQTS, where CALM2 evidence is strongest, e.g., PMIDs 23388215, 31283864, 30354306) may be graded below definitive, and several sources are single case reports or reviews restating background. Hence substantial probability remains on Existing, with little support for Hypothesized or Novel given clear human genetic data.

phenotype: cerebellar dysfunction with variable cognitive and behavioral abnormalities
justification: Multiple independent human cohorts report intragenic, single-nucleotide-level CAMTA1 variants in probands with cerebellar dysfunction, ataxia, developmental delay and behavioral abnormalities (CECBA). PMID 38044714 characterizes 26 new individuals with 23 novel CAMTA1 variants (frameshift, nonsense, splice, missense) and reviews 53 total cases; PMID 33131045 reports 10 individuals with nine previously unreported likely pathogenic variants; PMID 32157189 describes four patients with de novo nonsense, frameshift and missense variants causing ataxia/spasticity. These are supported by earlier reports of intragenic rearrangements causing non-progressive congenital ataxia (PMID 22693284) and single-case neuroimaging/phenotype and myoclonic dystonia reports (PMIDs 24145135, 33677721). Several listed papers (periodontitis, exercise VO2max, type 2 diabetes, neuroblastoma, fly dCAMTA) are unrelated or non-human and do not detract. The evidence is replicated across independent probands with point mutations, meeting the criteria for Established.

Weiss-Kruszka syndrome is a neurodevelopmental/craniofacial disorder caused by ZNF462 haploinsufficiency at 9q31, and none of the provided articles mention it. All the SYCP2L literature here concerns female reproductive ageing: GWAS loci for age at natural menopause (PMIDs 19448621, 23508249), variants influencing ovarian reserve and IVF outcomes (26099445, 37417852), homozygous variants causing premature ovarian insufficiency (32303603, 38521400), and a mouse knockout showing accelerated oocyte depletion (26362258). These phenotypes are unrelated to and not precursors of Weiss-Kruszka syndrome, and no mechanistic or pathway link is suggested. The co-mention is therefore incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles mention arterial tortuosity syndrome (classically caused by SLC2A10) or any vascular/connective tissue tortuosity phenotype. The ATP11C literature consistently supports roles in phosphatidylserine flippase activity with human disease associations limited to X-linked congenital hemolytic anemia, cholestasis/hyperbilirubinemia, iron overload, and B-lymphocyte development (PMIDs 42018644, 26944472, 31253392, 21423173, 21518881). Mouse and in vitro studies also address hepatocyte, placental, and erythrocyte membrane biology, not arterial wall integrity or elastogenesis. The Xq27 hypoparathyroidism papers involve ATP11C only by chromosomal location, with no mutations found, and are not relevant to arterial tortuosity. There is thus no logical or mechanistic basis linking ATP11C variation to arterial tortuosity syndrome, making "Novel" by far the most appropriate category.

Multiple human genetic reports directly implicate JMJD1C variants in neurodevelopmental phenotypes: Sáez et al. reported mutations in JMJD1C in Rett syndrome/intellectual disability patients (PMID 26181491), a splice-disrupting synonymous variant was linked to learning disability with myoclonic epilepsy (PMID 32996679), and de novo variants were found in seven unrelated patients with developmental delay/ID and seizures (PMID 31954878). However, that largest cohort explicitly notes plausible alternative explanations or modifying factors in every patient and concludes that further data are needed to support pathogenicity, which undercuts full "Established" status. Additional support is weak/indirect (an autism family pedigree candidate-gene screen, PMID 34368859) or non-neurodevelopmental/animal-based (leukemia, arthritis, neuropathic pain models). Thus the evidence is credible human genetic association but not definitively replicated as causal, favoring "Existing" with meaningful probability for "Established."

phenotype: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies
justification: Multiple independent human studies report point (non-CNV) variants in KIF4A in patients with neurodevelopmental phenotypes: Willemsen et al. identified KIF4A variants in X-linked intellectual disability families with synaptic functional support (PMID 24812067); a novel missense variant (p.Leu533Phe) segregated in four affected brothers with polymicrogyria, epilepsy and ID (PMID 39268972); the phenotype was expanded to include hydrocephalus, brain, renal/urogenital, lymphatic, eye and dental anomalies in additional probands (PMID 34346154); an additional pediatric case of XLID100 was reported (PMID 40372222); a fetal anomaly exome study identified a likely causal KIF4A variant (PMID 30679815); and a patient-derived R728Q variant was mechanistically validated in mice showing developmental delay and seizure susceptibility (PMID 36482480). These constitute replicated evidence in independent human probands/families with single-gene variants, precisely matching "complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies." Some remaining uncertainty stems from missense-variant interpretation caveats explicitly noted by the authors and from CNV-based reports (PMIDs 31085274, 33982443, 30298503) that cannot isolate KIF4A, so a small share is left for "Existing."

Multiple independent human genetic studies report ASAH1 variants identified directly in Farber lipogranulomatosis patients: PMID 24355074 characterized 13 ASAH1 mutations across 11 independent Farber families, PMID 10610716 identified three novel missense mutations (E138V, R254G, P362R) in patients with functional confirmation of reduced enzyme activity, PMID 10993717 uncovered four additional novel mutations, PMID 16951918 reported a novel missense mutation segregating in two affected siblings of an Indian family, and PMID 23707712 defined compound heterozygous splice and intragenic deletion alleles in a neonatal Farber case. Additional reports (34045195, 22565078, 40350404) confirm homozygous/novel ASAH1 variants in further probands, and allelic SMA-PME cases (22703880) extend the phenotypic spectrum. Mouse and cell models (30472209, 39665198, 34088014) provide supportive mechanistic evidence but are not required here. The evidence is replicated, human, and gene-specific, meeting the Established threshold.

Multiple primary human studies report pathogenic CAG repeat expansions in exon 1 of AR in independent Kennedy disease/SBMA probands and families: PMID 7702080 documents expansions in a large KD family, obligate carrier females, and sporadic motor neuron disease patients; PMID 30612224 identifies distinct expanded CAG alleles (48, 43, 44 repeats) in two Han Chinese families and one sporadic case; PMID 7699390 and 7515106 demonstrate expanded AR alleles and mutant AR transcripts in patient tissues and an autopsied SBMA spinal cord; PMID 26872663 reports a patient with 42 CAG repeats. Population-scale genomic screening (PMID 36797998) quantifies AR expansion frequency and estimated disease prevalence, and mutation databases (PMID 15146455) catalog SBMA-causing AR exon 1 expansions. Functional human work (PMID 8252045) shows reduced transactivation by polyQ-expanded AR, supporting mechanism. The evidence is human, replicated across independent probands and families, and mechanistically coherent, so the relationship is Established.

None of the provided articles address Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2E, which is a neurofilament light (NEFL)-related axonal neuropathy. The FKBP6 literature here concerns meiosis, synaptonemal complex formation, piRNA biogenesis and male infertility/azoospermia (PMIDs 12764197, 36150389, 16227348, 17307919), Williams-Beuren syndrome contiguous gene deletions (PMID 20049703), and incidental CNV/exome associations in congenital heart disease and cancer cohorts (PMIDs 22318994, 42315506). No peripheral nerve, axonal degeneration, or CMT phenotype is described, and no mechanistic pathway link to neurofilament biology or hereditary neuropathy is suggested. Therefore the gene–phenotype relationship is best described as Novel, with only a negligible chance of a hypothesized biological link.

None of the provided articles report gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Swyer syndrome, streak gonads, 46,XY/46,XX DSD) in association with MT-CO3. The clinically informative MT-CO3 papers describe entirely different phenotypes: MELAS (PMID 34054915), rhabdomyolysis (PMIDs 41679129, 21163656), LHON-like optic neuropathy (PMID 37808372), epilepsy (PMID 37095367), and pediatric mitochondrial disease (PMIDs 36918699, 32348839). The closest reproductive links are indirect and weak: a PCOS mtDNA sequencing study noting heteroplasmic variants frequently in MT-CO3 (PMID 36563715), and a sperm-quality study that explicitly found no association between MT-CO1/2/3 variants and semen parameters (PMID 40038427); PCOS and impaired spermatogenesis are not gonadal dysgenesis. Thus there is no genetic or mechanistic evidence connecting MT-CO3 to gonadal dysgenesis, only a tenuous "gonadal/mitochondrial energy metabolism" rationale supporting a small Hypothesized weight.

No articles were provided, so there is no evidence of any kind linking APC to complement component 2 deficiency. APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) is a Wnt-pathway tumor suppressor associated with familial adenomatous polyposis, whereas complement component 2 deficiency is caused by variants in the C2 gene within the MHC class III region; there is no shared biology or pathway rationale. The acronym "APC" is also commonly used for activated protein C or antigen-presenting cells, which could generate incidental co-mentions with complement biology, but such homonym usage would not constitute gene-level evidence. Absent any human genetic, functional, or model-organism data, the relationship is best classified as Novel.

phenotype: arthrogryposis, distal, with impaired proprioception and touch
justification: None of the provided articles mention arthrogryposis, distal arthrogryposis, or impaired proprioception/touch (a phenotype classically caused by PIEZO2 variants). Human genetic reports on RBFOX3 concern rolandic/generalized epilepsy (PMID 24039908, 34039076, 40011789), sleep latency (PMID 27142678), cleft lip/palate association (PMID 23512105), serum urate (PMID 25811787), and developmental delay/speech disorders via chromosomal breakpoints (PMID 24603971) — none relate to a distal arthrogryposis or somatosensory phenotype. Animal and molecular work (PMID 26619789, 35951651) shows RBFOX3 regulates neuronal excitability and splicing in CNS neurons, which offers only a very generic, non-specific biological rationale for sensory-neuron involvement, not evidence for this phenotype. Remaining papers use RBFOX3/NeuN merely as a neuronal marker, i.e., incidental co-mention. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel, with a small allowance for a speculative biological (Hypothesized) link.

nearest_curated_disease: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, and absent language
justification: None of the provided articles link PSMB1 variants to glycogen storage disease III, which is caused by AGL (glycogen debranching enzyme) deficiency. PSMB1 evidence in humans concerns proteasomopathies with microcephaly, intellectual disability, and developmental delay (PMID: 32129449, 38866022), plus a multigene 6q terminal deletion (PMID: 26929909) unrelated to glycogen metabolism. Other papers cover zebrafish craniofacial development, transcriptional roles in RBP4/VMAT2 promoters, senescence, and cardiac hypertrophy; the only "glycogen" mention is glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK-3) in the zonisamide study (PMID: 38097716), an incidental term, not the disease. Thus the co-mentions are incidental with no mechanistic or genetic basis for a PSMB1–GSD III relationship.

None of the provided articles mention lipoprotein metabolism, apolipoprotein B, or hypobetalipoproteinemia in any form. CDH15 (M-cadherin) literature centers on intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental phenotypes (often within multigene 16q24.3 CNVs), myogenesis and muscle mass, plasma proteomic QTLs, and DNA methylation biomarkers. There is no genetic, functional, or pathway-based rationale connecting CDH15 to familial hypobetalipoproteinemia 1, which is classically caused by APOB variants. A small residual probability is assigned to Hypothesized only because CDH15's role in muscle/metabolic tissue biology could be loosely construed as metabolically relevant, but no direct link exists.

Every retrieved article links ANO3 exclusively to dystonia phenotypes (DYT24/craniocervical dystonia, tremulous dystonia, dyskinetic encephalopathy), with functional work on Ca2+ signalling and phospholipid scramblase activity in neurons. None of the abstracts mentions arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, congenital contractures, fetal akinesia, or a neurogenic congenital contracture phenotype, and none reports patients with AMC2. There is thus no human genetic evidence and no credible biological rationale presented connecting ANO3 to arthrogryposis multiplex congenita 2, neurogenic type. A small residual probability is left for "hypothesized" because ANO3 is a neuronally expressed ion channel/scramblase affecting excitability, which could in principle be argued relevant to neurogenic motor phenotypes, but this is speculative and unsupported by the listed literature.

Every provided article concerns SCN9A (NaV1.7) in nociception-related phenotypes: erythromelalgia/erythermalgia, paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, congenital insensitivity to pain, small fiber neuropathy, and familial episodic pain syndromes. None of the abstracts mentions hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, GnRH neuron biology, puberty, or reproductive endocrine phenotypes. The only tenuous conceptual bridge is that SCN9A loss of function can co-occur with anosmia (a feature of Kallmann syndrome), but no article here reports olfactory or reproductive findings, so this remains speculative and unsupported. There are no human genetic studies linking SCN9A variants to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in this corpus, precluding Existing or Established. A small residual probability is given to Hypothesized on the basis of the channel's expression in sensory/olfactory neurons.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with spastic quadriplegia, optic atrophy, seizures, and structural brain anomalies
justification: None of the provided articles report patients with neurodevelopmental disorder featuring spastic quadriplegia, optic atrophy, seizures, and structural brain anomalies, and no probands or families with SELENBP1 variants causing this phenotype are described. The only human Mendelian phenotype documented is extraoral halitosis from methanethiol oxidase deficiency (PMID 29255262), a non-neurological metabolic condition, and the remaining human genetic work concerns schizophrenia association/expression studies (PMIDs 16223876, 18163446, 19596560, 20615253) plus an incidental keratoconus candidate-gene list (PMID 42162727). However, biological plausibility exists: SELENBP1 is robustly expressed in human cortex, and a transgenic mouse overexpressing human SELENBP1 shows cortical heterotopia/ectopia-like malformations, altered pyramidal neuron excitability and abnormal EEG (PMID 36512497), features conceptually adjacent to structural brain anomalies and seizures; its role in H2S/methanethiol metabolism is also neurologically relevant (PMIDs 33901808, 35316559). This supports Hypothesized over Existing/Established, with meaningful residual probability that the co-mentions are entirely incidental (Novel).

Malan overgrowth syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of NFIX (19p13.2), and none of the provided articles report CACNA1F variants in patients with overgrowth, macrocephaly, or Malan syndrome. All CACNA1F literature here concerns X-linked incomplete congenital stationary night blindness, Aland Island eye disease, and related retinal/optic nerve phenotypes, plus mouse/rat models of Cav1.4 synaptopathy. The only tangential item is a systematic review of calcium channelopathies and intellectual disability (PMID 33985586), which discusses ID/GDD broadly but does not implicate CACNA1F in Malan overgrowth syndrome; shared nonspecific features such as developmental delay do not constitute a mechanistic link. Therefore the co-mentions are incidental and the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for a weak biological (neurodevelopmental calcium signaling) rationale.

nearest_curated_disease: congenital disorder of glycosylation, type IIy
justification: Deafness-lymphedema-leukemia syndrome (Emberger syndrome) is a GATA2-related disorder, and none of the provided articles link GET4 to deafness, lymphedema, or leukemia. The only human variant report for GET4 (PMID 32395830) describes compound heterozygous missense variants causing global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and dysmorphism via disruption of the TRC/tail-anchored protein targeting pathway — an entirely different phenotype. Other papers (PMIDs 35262690, 34060591, 38467609, 26451041, 28973888, 20850366) address GET4 biochemistry in the GET/TRC pathway, proteasome function, MERCS, or non-human organisms, with no mechanistic or phenotypic relevance to hearing loss, lymphatic dysfunction, or myeloid malignancy. No causal or associative human genetic evidence exists for this gene–phenotype pair, so the co-mentions are incidental.

nearest_curated_disease: joint contractures, osteochondromas, and B-cell lymphoma
justification: No article reports NFATC2 variants in patients with spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, 'corner fracture' type (a disorder classically caused by FN1 variants); thus Established cannot be supported, as no PMID here describes probands with this phenotype and NFATC2 variants. The strongest human genetic evidence is a single individual with biallelic NFATC2 loss-of-function presenting joint contractures, osteochondromas, and lymphoma (PMID 35789258) — a skeletal phenotype but a distinct entity, giving only partial support to "Existing". Biological plausibility is substantial: NFATp/NFATC2 acts as a repressor of chondrogenesis and its loss in mice produces ectopic cartilage and endochondral ossification (PMID 10620601), and NFATC2 participates in osteoclast/bone signaling (PMIDs 15759284, 32742319), supporting a Hypothesized relationship to skeletal dysplasia. A curious but incidental link is an FN1-NFATc2 fusion in synovial chondromatosis (PMID 31589790), involving the SMDCF gene FN1 but not implicating NFATC2 variants in the dysplasia itself. Most remaining articles concern immunity, melanoma, or neurons and are irrelevant.

phenotype: epidermolysis bullosa simplex 4, localized or generalized intermediate, autosomal recessive
justification: All provided articles concern KCNE2 exclusively as a cardiac/neuronal voltage-gated potassium channel β-subunit, addressing long-QT syndrome, atrial fibrillation, sudden unexplained death, and channel trafficking/interactions with KCNH2, KCNQ1, and Kv4.3. None mentions epidermolysis bullosa simplex, skin fragility, keratin genes (KRT5/KRT14), hemidesmosomes, or any dermatological phenotype. EBS4 (localized or generalized intermediate, autosomal recessive) is attributed to biallelic KRT14 variants, and no biological pathway linking KCNE2 to keratinocyte cytoskeletal integrity is presented in these abstracts. There is therefore no direct, indirect, or mechanistic evidence connecting KCNE2 to this phenotype, warranting a "Novel" classification.

phenotype: autosomal recessive mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial diseases due to complete RORgamma receptor deficiency
justification: Every article provided links RPL3L to cardiac and skeletal muscle phenotypes—neonatal dilated cardiomyopathy type 2D, atrial fibrillation, muscle development—or to unrelated conditions such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia and collagen VI dystrophies. None mentions Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, RORC/RORgamma deficiency, or any immunological/IL-17-related phenotype. RPL3L is a muscle-restricted ribosomal protein paralogue with no described role in Th17 immunity or mycobacterial defence, so there is not even a plausible biological pathway link in this literature. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only incidental co-mention potential.

nearest_curated_disease: intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal recessive 80, with variant lissencephaly
justification: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome corresponds to the CASP2-related autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with lissencephaly/pachygyria. PMID 37880421 reports primary evidence: seven patients from five independent families with biallelic truncating CASP2 variants (homozygous and compound heterozygous), with segregation and RNA splicing validation. PMID 39672921 provides an independent additional case that replicates and expands the clinical spectrum. Supporting biological plausibility comes from the PIDDosome pathway, where CRADD and PIDD1 biallelic variants cause an overlapping lissencephaly phenotype (PMIDs 27773430, 37716905). Since at least two human reports with distinct probands demonstrate causal single-gene variants, Established is favored, with residual weight on Existing given the still-limited number of reported families.

Autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss 59 (DFNB59) is attributed to PJVK, and none of the provided articles report biallelic AMIGO2 variants in deaf probands. The only hearing-loss co-mention is a multigene proximal 12q deletion case (PMID 15362574), where the authors themselves attributed the hearing loss and cleft palate to COL2A1, not AMIGO2; a CNV spanning many genes cannot implicate AMIGO2 anyway, and a second 12q13.11 microdeletion report (PMID 20933621) links AMIGO2 only to intellectual disability. AMIGO2 variants have been reported in oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum (PMIDs 31074142, 33530447), a syndromic craniofacial/ear malformation phenotype that is distinct from nonsyndromic recessive sensorineural deafness, providing at most weak indirect biological plausibility. The remaining literature concerns cancer metastasis, PDK1/Akt signaling, cardiac ischemia, and neuronal adhesion/axon fasciculation, with no cochlear or auditory relevance, so the evidence best supports "Novel" with some residual weight for a hypothesized ear-development link.

Both provided articles concern KCND3 (Kv4.3) as a cardiac potassium channel candidate gene for long QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome, with SNP surveys and genomic organisation/chromosomal mapping. Neither mentions gonadal development, sex determination, or 46,XY sex reversal in any form. There is no expression, pathway, animal model, or variant-level evidence linking KCND3 to disorders of sex development. The co-mentions are entirely incidental, supporting a "Novel" classification.

Every article provided links KCNQ4 to autosomal dominant non-syndromic sensorineural hearing loss (DFNA2), age-related hearing loss, or potassium channel function in the inner ear. None mention skeletal dysplasia, spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, X-linked skeletal phenotypes, or bone/cartilage biology. KCNQ4 is an autosomal gene (chromosome 1p34), which is inconsistent with an X-linked disorder. There is no biological pathway, expression, or animal-model evidence in these papers connecting KCNQ4 to skeletal development. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

phenotype: arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with wooly hair and keratoderma
justification: Every provided article concerns NBEAL2 in the context of gray platelet syndrome, α-granule biogenesis, megakaryocyte/platelet biology, and immune cell (neutrophil, NK, mast cell, T cell) function. None mentions cardiomyopathy, woolly hair, palmoplantar keratoderma, or desmosomal biology (the JUP/DSP/PKP2 pathways underlying Naxos and Carvajal syndromes). There are no human probands or families linking NBEAL2 variants to arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, and no animal or mechanistic data suggesting cardiac or ectodermal involvement. The co-mention of gene and phenotype is therefore incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

All provided literature links TSPEAR to autosomal recessive ectodermal dysplasia type 14 (dental/hair anomalies) and to nonsyndromic sensorineural hearing loss (DFNB98), with functional roles in Notch/Wnt signaling in skin, tooth, and inner ear. No article mentions tibial muscular dystrophy, distal myopathy, skeletal muscle phenotypes, or TTN-related disease. There is also no plausible biological pathway connecting TSPEAR's ectodermal/cochlear function to muscular dystrophy, and animal models (zebrafish, mouse knockouts) show no muscle phenotype. Therefore the gene–phenotype relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a negligible allowance for hypothesized biology.

None of the supplied articles report atrial septal defect (ASD6) probands or families with TNNT2 variants; the entire corpus concerns hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive and thin-filament cardiomyopathies, so there are no two independent human studies demonstrating a causal TNNT2–ASD6 link and "Established" cannot be supported from this evidence. The closest atrial-related human data are TNNT2 mutation carriers with left atrial dilation and atrial fibrillation (PMID 35514357), which involves atrial myopathy rather than septal malformation, and the mechanistic work in that study is largely in mouse models, pushing weight toward "Hypothesized". TNNT2's biology—an essential cardiac sarcomeric thin-filament protein expressed throughout cardiac development, with clear human disease-causing variant burden (PMIDs 8989109, 11862580, 24111713, 36252119)—provides a plausible but indirect basis for a congenital cardiac structural defect. Some residual probability is retained for "Existing" because curated resources list TNNT2 under ASD6 based on literature not included here, and a small probability for "Novel" because co-mention in this list is purely incidental to cardiomyopathy.

Every article provided concerns PCCA/PCCB variants causing propionic acidemia, an organic acidemia due to propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, with no mention of bile acid metabolism, hypercholanemia, or elevated serum bile salts. Familial hypercholanemia type 2 is attributed to SLC10A1 (NTCP) deficiency, a bile acid uptake transporter unrelated to PCCA's mitochondrial carboxylase function. None of the abstracts report cholestasis, bile acid measurements, or pruritus phenotypes in PCCA patients, and no genetic study links PCCA variants to hypercholanemia. The co-mention of PCCA with metabolic/liver topics (e.g., liver transplantation in propionic acidemia) is incidental and provides no mechanistic basis for hypercholanemia. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel, with a small residual allowance for a hypothesized hepatic-metabolic link.

All retrieved articles concern STXBP2 in familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis type 5, microvillus inclusion disease/congenital diarrheal disorders, inflammatory bowel disease, EBV susceptibility, and anterior uveitis — none report hearing loss phenotypes or any auditory involvement. No paper describes STXBP2 variants in probands or families with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss 44 (DFNB44), and there is no cochlear expression or inner-ear functional/animal-model evidence presented. The gene's known biology (SNARE-mediated cytotoxic granule exocytosis and epithelial vesicular trafficking) provides no specific mechanistic bridge to nonsyndromic deafness. Therefore the co-mention is incidental, supporting a Novel classification, with only trace probability assigned to a speculative biological link.

nearest_curated_disease: mitochondrial complex III deficiency, nuclear type 11
justification: None of the provided articles report hereditary spastic paraplegia 45 (an NT5C2-related disorder) in association with UQCRH. The only human genetic evidence (PMID 34750991) links a homozygous UQCRH two-exon deletion to isolated mitochondrial complex III deficiency presenting with lactic acidosis, hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy, not spastic paraplegia; the mouse and AOX studies (PMID 37230398) address the same complex III phenotype. Other papers involve incidental co-mentions in proteomics, cancer, Parkinson's PARK10 mapping, and retinal degeneration. A weak residual case for "hypothesized" exists only because mitochondrial OXPHOS dysfunction can broadly cause neurodegenerative/spastic phenotypes, but no direct link to HSP45 is presented. Therefore the relationship is best classified as novel.

nearest_curated_disease: obesity due to melanocortin 4 receptor deficiency
justification: All three articles concern MC4R's canonical roles in energy homeostasis/obesity (PMID 33795520), reproductive function via kisspeptin neurons (PMID 40674128), and ovarian teratoma susceptibility in mouse congenic strains (PMID 33568756). None mention B-cell development, immunoglobulin production, immunodeficiency, or agammaglobulinemia, and none report human patients with humoral immune defects. There is no biological pathway link presented between melanocortin 4 receptor signaling and autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia 2 (typically caused by IGLL1 and related B-cell receptor genes). The co-mentions are entirely incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

phenotype: congenital myopathy 2c, severe infantile, autosomal dominant
justification: No article in this set reports CDK9 variants in patients with congenital myopathy 2C (a disorder classically attributed to ACTA1), so Established is untenable — there are zero PMIDs describing probands or families with CDK9 variants. The only myopathy-relevant item (PMID 11373316) maps cyclin T2a, a CDK9 partner, to 2q21 near myopathy loci and reports loss of cyclin T2a immunostaining in two centronuclear myopathy cases, suggesting a speculative biological involvement of the CDK9–cyclin T2a complex in muscle disease; this is indirect, concerns a different myopathy subtype, and involves the partner cyclin rather than CDK9 variants. All remaining papers are about CDK9/P-TEFb in transcription elongation, HIV Tat, cancer, or unrelated neurodevelopmental disease, and are incidental to the phenotype. This supports a Hypothesized relationship at best, with substantial probability that the link is entirely incidental (Novel).

None of the provided articles link PHGDH to Joubert syndrome 33, a ciliopathy defined by the molar tooth sign; the human genetic evidence for PHGDH concerns serine biosynthesis defects (phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency, Neu-Laxova spectrum) presenting with congenital microcephaly, seizures and psychomotor retardation (PMIDs 28440900, 33565074, 37347880). Animal work (Phgdh knockout mice with brain malformation, PMID 18296366) supports a role in CNS development, which provides only a nonspecific biological rationale for a neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than for the JBTS33 cerebellar/ciliary phenotype. Remaining papers concern cancer metabolism, macrophage immunometabolism, Alzheimer's disease, and gout, and are irrelevant. No probands or families with Joubert syndrome carrying PHGDH variants are reported, so Established and Existing cannot be supported; the modest Hypothesized weight reflects the shared brain-malformation/microcephaly biology.

phenotype: intellectual developmental disorder with macrocephaly, seizures, and speech delay
justification: Direct human genetic evidence with patient-level variants is reported in multiple independent studies: PMID 31504246 identified de novo heterozygous missense PAK1 variants in four unrelated individuals with intellectual disability, macrocephaly and seizures, with functional modelling supporting gain of function; PMID 36905087 reports an additional de novo p.Leu470Gln variant in the kinase domain, noting seven previously reported de novo variants; PMID 41516310 adds a novel de novo p.Asn132Lys variant in a further proband; and PMID 37102288 describes another child with epilepsy, developmental delay and a PAK1 variant. These are single-nucleotide/missense variants in independent probands, not multigene copy-number changes, satisfying replication requirements. Supporting biology (oligodendroglial/neurodevelopmental roles, PAK group I regulation of brain development) is consistent with pathogenicity but is secondary to the human data.

Two human case reports present their own primary data implicating MT-TC (mt-tRNA-Cys) variants in mitochondrial disease phenotypes: a novel MT-TC variant in a patient with MERRF and intranuclear inclusions (PMID 34433719), and a late-onset MELAS patient with m.5783G>A, which lies within MT-TC (PMID 38881794). These are independent probands, supporting at least an "Existing" and arguably "Established" relationship, but both are single-patient reports with limited functional/segregation confirmation. Notably, PMID 18800376 explicitly warns that MT-TC variants have often been over-called as "novel" and "pathogenic" without adequate database/haplogroup evaluation, and PMID 25923817 concludes an MT-TC variant (m.5772G>A) in HCM patients is not pathogenic, tempering the strength of the evidence. Other listed papers are general reviews or non-human plant/fish mitogenome studies (trnC homonym) and contribute nothing. Overall, evidence supports a credible but not definitively replicated causal role, so "Existing" is favored over "Established."

The original discovery study (PMID 28092684) identified biallelic loss-of-function TOE1 variants in 12 independent human families with PCH7, with zebrafish modeling support. Numerous independent clinical reports have since replicated the association with novel compound heterozygous variants in unrelated probands: a Chinese patient (34716526), a Japanese patient with an NLM variant (38605133), a Chinese pedigree with prenatal diagnosis (37635087), a Korean boy (37945020), a Chinese family with affected siblings (37608778), and additional cases (36738896, 38596058, 41847829). Multicentric PCH cohort studies (34085948, 38347586) further support gene–phenotype correlation, and biochemical work shows PCH7 mutations impair TOE1 stability and exonuclease activity. This constitutes strong, replicated human genetic evidence for causation.

Multiple independent human studies report their own primary genetic findings of PLS3 point/frameshift/splice variants segregating with early-onset X-linked osteoporosis and fractures: PMID 38043102 (five new families with stop-gain variants), PMID 28605746 (two new families with novel mutations), PMID 25209159 (novel splice mutation c.73-24T>A segregating in a large family), PMID 24616189 (two families with p.Asp332* and p.Leu478Pro), PMID 29884797 (de novo frameshift c.1096_1100delAACTT), and PMID 40353206 (28 patients from 11 families, each with a distinct PLS3 variant). These are independent probands/families with single-gene sequence variants, not multigene deletions, providing replicated causal evidence in humans. Additional cohort (PMID 39316135) and functional/mechanistic work (PMID 28646489) and biomarker/phenotyping studies further support the relationship. Therefore the gene–disease relationship is Established.

Two independent discovery papers established causality in humans: Briggs et al. (PMID 21217755) mapped the locus to 19p13 with linkage (LOD 3.6) and found biallelic ACP5 mutations in ten individuals from eight families, and Lausch et al. (PMID 21217752) independently identified ACP5 mutations in 14 affected individuals from five consanguineous families with loss of TRAP enzyme activity. Replication comes from a comprehensive molecularly confirmed cohort survey (PMID 26951490), five new Egyptian patients with three novel variants (PMID 37010587), and numerous additional independent probands with novel biallelic variants (PMIDs 26346816, 33712926, 27718324, 26789720, 38883133). Functional data (loss of TRAP activity, osteopontin accumulation, type I interferon signature) supply a coherent mechanism. The evidence is unambiguous and replicated in humans, warranting Established.

The strongest evidence is PMID 37013900, which reports de novo MRTFB variants in patients with a novel neurodevelopmental phenotype with dysmorphic features, supported by gain-of-function modeling in Drosophila. Independent human genetic support comes from PMID 29463886, where a novel loss-of-function MKL2 (MRTFB) variant was identified in childhood apraxia of speech, a neurodevelopmental speech disorder, and PMID 23692340, reporting a rare deleterious MKL2 variant with a cis-deletion in three sisters with extreme fatal microcephaly. Older candidate-gene/linkage studies (PMIDs 15830322, 20442744) report only weak or unreplicated association of MKL2 with autism. Additional supportive but non-causal biology includes MRTFB's role in dendritic morphology, SRF-mediated transcription, and neural crest/brain development (PMIDs 34795561, 41320266, 16204380). Because the strongest single report is one cohort study and the corroborating human reports involve differing phenotypes or single families, probability is split roughly evenly between Established and Existing.

The strongest primary evidence is Hawn et al. (PMID 16027372), a human family-based TDT study showing the TLR5 C1174T (392STOP) allele is protectively associated with SLE, with supporting functional cytokine data. Additional human genetic studies report TLR5 variant associations in specific populations (PMID 26221343 in Zhuang/Han Chinese; PMID 28763101 where rs5744168 associated with lupus nephritis though not SLE overall), but replication attempts in Caucasian American (PMID 17516623) and Spanish (PMID 19473567) cohorts were largely negative, and meta-analyses (PMIDs 22325161, 26762473) do not establish a consistent effect. This inconsistent replication precludes "Established," since no two independent studies convincingly demonstrate a causal role in their own results. Remaining supportive material is expression/pathway-level (PMIDs 19843090, 18373699, 26592511), which would only support "Hypothesized." Therefore "Existing" is the best fit.

The strongest primary human evidence is Schönberger et al. (PMID 15735644), which identified an intragenic ~4.8 kb EYA4 deletion producing a truncated 193-aa peptide segregating with dilated cardiomyopathy and SNHL in a family previously mapped to 6q23-24 (PMID 10769282), supported by zebrafish morpholino and biochemical work. Additional human support is thinner: a Japanese patient with an EYA4 variant showed only minor, asymptomatic ECG/echocardiographic abnormalities (PMID 30155266), and a small pediatric cardiomyopathy cohort listed EYA4 among DCM-associated genes in one patient (PMID 41270882), but with minimal segregation or phenotypic detail. Counterbalancing reports show many EYA4 truncating alleles cause nonsyndromic DFNA10 hearing loss with formally normal cardiac evaluation (PMIDs 17567890, 25681523), indicating incomplete/position-dependent cardiac penetrance. Mouse/zebrafish functional data (PMID 26499333, 22971774) reinforce biological plausibility but are non-human. Because robust, well-characterized independent human families with DCM are essentially limited to one report, "Existing" is favored over "Established," though the latter remains plausible.
